runs.text:
A quotation is a room built inside another room:
smaller, quieter, and entered on purpose.
-- A Reader

Every page carries at least two voices: the one that argues and
the one that answers. The second voice often lives in the margin,
set smaller than the body so the eye can choose which line to
follow. A book that hides the second voice pretends the argument
was always alone, and a book that enlarges it drowns the first.

The typesetter knows this trade-off well. A footnote is a whisper
at the foot of the page; a block quote is a pause in the middle of
the claim, and an epigraph is the door left ajar before the chapter
begins. Each one asks the reader to slow down without asking the
reader to stop.

To read slowly is not to read less. It is to let each sentence
finish its work before the next one starts, and to notice when a
quotation has been set apart from the claim it serves.

The margin is where the two voices agree to
live apart. One keeps the claim moving forward,
the other keeps the claim honest, and neither
pretends to be the other. A reader who skips
the margin loses the argument the margin saved.

When the quote ends, the body returns at the same size it left,
and the argument picks up the thread. Nothing was lost in the
detour; something was proved by it.
